Reviewed initial benchmark results, discussed caching and batching tradeoffs, and agreed on next benchmark runs to quantify tokens/sec and tokens/$ across batch sizes and caching strategies. Action items assigned to run larger throughput tests, share logs for better cost modelling, and prepare a dedicated capacity trial conversation if economics look favorable.
transcript:
Meeting header: 2025-02-12 15:00 PST (45m) attendees: Jordan Kim (Redwood AE), Priya Singh (Redwood SE), Alex Rivera (Redwood CSM); Sam Rodriguez (Acme CTO), Maya Chen (ML Eng), Liam O'Neil (Infra), Nora Patel (Product)

Summary: quick recap of last week, went over small benchmark deck Jordan sent, dug into tokens/sec per dollar, caching numbers looked promising but need larger run, decided to run 100k token benchmark with different batch sizes and caching on/off.

[00:00] Jordan: alright uh thanks everyone for joining, um this is the weekly POC sync for Acme. quick agenda: go over the numbers Priya ran, talk caching and batching tradeoffs, agree next benchmark and who's doing what. Sam, Maya, you still good with this agenda?
[00:18] Sam: yep sounds good. we mainly want to validate cost numbers, like tokens per dollar and what caching buys us in our workload.
[00:25] Priya: cool, I ran the small pilot last night — 20k token window across three models: redwood-v2-small (quantized), redwood-v2-medium (int8), and a larger non-quantized baseline. note: some of the model names might be off in the logs, transcription hates capitalization.
[00:40] Maya: quick question before you dive in — when you say tokens/$ are you normalizing for latency SLO? our product needs p95 < 300ms for interactive flows.
[00:50] Priya: good point, yes the initial table had both tokens/sec and tokens/$ and we included p50/p95 in separate cols. for the quantized path we saw tokens/sec improve ~1.6x vs baseline, tokens/$ improved ~2.1x but p95 increased about 40ms on average.
[01:10] Liam: oh can you repeat the cache assumption? you said prefix caching was on?
[01:14] Priya: right, prefix caching (we call it prefix/KV caching) used for repeated context. in the run with caching enabled, effective tokens generated per second increased because we didn't re-run the prefix. savings depend on hit rate — I used a simulated 35% hit rate based on your sample prompts.
[01:30] Sam: 35% is reasonable, our prompts have a lot of shared boilerplate. sometimes we'll see higher when sessions reuse system prompts.
[01:38] Jordan: to put numbers on it, the caching run moved tokens/sec from 220 to about 320 on the medium model at batch size 8. tokens/$ went from about 0.00045 to 0.0003 (so lower cost per token). those are the quick numbers in the deck.
[01:55] Nora: that sounds promising, what about batching? we worry about tail latency for user-facing flows.
[02:02] Priya: yes batching helps tokens/sec and amortizes kernel launch overhead. in our tests batch sizes 1,4,8,16 were evaluated. throughput increased up to batch 8, after that p95 jumped significantly especially on the bigger models. so there's a sweet spot — for your latency SLO I'd recommend batch 4 or 8 with dynamic batching enabled.
[02:25] Maya: is dynamic batching something you enable at the request router level? how does it play with dedicated capacity?
[02:32] Jordan: yeah dynamic batching is part of the serving runtime. on Dedicated we can tune batching windows and max batch size per GPU pool. Dedicated gives more predictable throughput so you can push batch sizes a bit more aggressively if you accept slightly higher tail latency.
[02:45] Sam: and what's the effect of quantization here? you mentioned int8 and 4bit in the doc.
[02:50] Priya: int8 gave the best cost/latency tradeoff in our runs — about 1.6x tokens/sec and minimal accuracy delta on your eval prompt set. 4bit (we tried a mixed 4/8 profile) gets you more cost savings but some regression on generation quality for edge prompts. we can run targeted evals on your top 50 prompts to quantify regression.
[03:12] Jordan: actionably, the plan is to do a larger scale benchmark to get tokens/sec/$ curves across batch sizes and caching hit rates.
[03:20] Maya: what about KV cache vs prefix cache wording? I think sometimes your notes call it KV cash (laughs) — we've seen different cache types in other infra.
[03:28] Priya: ha yeah transcription. to be clear: KV cache refers to key/value cache for autoregressive decoding (reuse decoder states), prefix cache means skipping the prefix conditioning pass. both help, KV cache helps across continuing sessions, prefix caching if large shared system prompts are used.
[03:44] Liam: any concerns about memory with KV cache on larger models? we have GPU memory limits in our Dedicated test cluster.
[03:50] Priya: absolutely — KV cache increases memory footprint linearly with sequence length and batch. that's why our medium model with batch 8 hit 80% memory on the 48GB GPU. we can recommend a per-GPU slot config or auto-eviction policies; for dedicated trials we can size the pool differently.
[04:10] Jordan: quick pause — Maya, for the cost model spreadsheet we asked for your prompt mix and sample logs. did you have that or need more time?
[04:18] Maya: I'm assembling anonymized logs now. I can send 3 days of traffic and the top 50 prompts by next monday.
[04:24] Jordan: perfect. Alex will share our cost spreadsheet so you can plug them in.
[04:28] Alex: I'll drop the sheet after the call with the assumptions tabbed out: batch assumptions, cache hit rate, model unit cost, p95 targets.
[04:36] Sam: about competitors, we've been comparing against OpenAI's API for latency and Anthropic for safety eval. cost-wise Vertex AI looked similar on paper but less flexible on batching controls. just FYI.
[04:50] Priya: good to know. for the dedicated conversation we can show a committed monthly cost vs on-demand pricing and expected tokens/sec under your peak.
[04:58] Nora: what about security & compliance — any blockers for the dedicated path?
[05:02] Jordan: no blockers — we have Private (VPC/on-prem) options, SOC2 docs, KMS integrations. Alex will send the security pack. if you need air-gapped, we have an on-prem package but that's a longer engagement.
[05:16] Maya: back to numbers — can you share the exact table rows you used for tokens/$ calculation? e.g. how you price GPU seconds, amortized model load, cache savings per hit.
[05:27] Priya: yes the spreadsheet breaks it down: model compute $/GPU-second, amortized model load per request (negligible with caching), network egress, and cache hit reduces compute by the prefix cost. example: a 35% hit rate reduced token compute cost by roughly 28% in our sim.
[05:45] Sam: those are the kind of numbers we need to justify Dedicated commit. if Dedicated would lower tokens/$ by 30-40% given our peak, that's interesting.
[05:56] Jordan: our preliminary sim shows Dedicated with reserved capacity + larger batch sizes could give you 25-40% cost reduction depending on cache hit and model choice. we'll quantify in the next run.
[06:06] Maya: can you include p99 in the next run? for us p99 spikes are a killer during peak usage.
[06:12] Priya: yes we'll capture p50/p95/p99 and tail distribution for each config.
[06:18] Liam: are you planning to run the next benchmark on Hosted or Dedicated infra? memory behavior differs.
[06:23] Priya: we'll run both if possible — first on Hosted where we've been running, then on a small Dedicated test pool so you can see the delta. Dedicated run will also include specialized kernel config and potentially alternative compilation kernels.
[06:36] Jordan: timeline: benchmark run this week, results early next week. share results and then meet to decide on a 2-week Dedicated trial.
[06:44] Sam: sounds good. for the Dedicated trial we will need a simple SLA ask: <5% downtime and p95 targets. is that standard?
[06:53] Jordan: SLA is configurable per contract; our Dedicated offering includes an SLA and operational playbook. Alex will follow up with the SLA template.
[07:02] Maya: small nit — when you report tokens/$ please also give cost per completed request for our event-based billing analysis. we have variable response lengths.
[07:11] Priya: will do — we'll show both cost/token and cost/request with average and 95th percentile response length.
[07:18] Nora: anything else on security or procurement?
[07:21] Sam: procurement wants an initial T&C draft if we move to Dedicated. we can start that in parallel.
[07:27] Jordan: noted. Alex will surface procurement contacts and template.
[07:31] Priya: okay I think that's the main meat. I'll run the batch sweep (1/4/8/16) with caching on/off and quant profiles (int8/4bit) and capture p50/p95/p99, tokens/sec and tokens/$.
[07:44] Maya: thanks. also please mark which runs exceed memory thresholds so we don't propose unfeasible configs.
[07:49] Priya: yes will do. I'll annotate memory usage and if batch+seq length hits > GPU memory we'll log the failure.
[07:56] Jordan: quick recap and next steps: Jordan/Priya run the large benchmark, Alex send the spreadsheet and security docs, Maya share logs, then reconvene next week to review.
[08:08] Sam: great thanks everyone.
[08:10] Jordan: thanks all. end.

Notes: transcription imperfect in spots (model names and some acronyms); references to 'KV cash' in transcript are 'KV cache'. Attached artifacts referenced: benchmark deck (link: https://redwood.ai/poc/acme/bench-deck - internal), cost-model spreadsheet (will be shared), security pack link (will be shared).
